meta.title: Hebrew B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hebrew → English (see the Hebrew, recall the meaning) and English → Hebrew (see an English meaning, recall the Hebrew). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in their field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. The Hebrew taught is the modern standard language of Israel. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hebrew, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 110 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — politics and public administration, the law and the courts, the economy and finance, science and research, technology, the environment and natural resources, health and the mind, the arts, literature and the media, history and society, argument and evaluation — the words for claims, evidence, causes and consequences — the formal connectors of written Hebrew, and the verbs of reporting, analysing and persuading — and the other 1390 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Hebrew, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, including the forms written with a prefix such as ו "and", ה "the" or ב "in" joined to the front. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed as Hebrew is normally written — without vowel points, in the full spelling — with the POINTED form beneath it, which shows how it is said, and Wiktionary's romanisation with the stress marked (shalóm, katáv). Words spelt alike are separate cards where the level teaches both (שֵׁם "name", שָׁם "there"). The Hebrew Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters and the vowel points. The 866 nouns show their gender and plural; the 386 verbs are given, as Hebrew dictionaries give them, in the past tense "he" form, with their infinitive, present, future and binyan (the verb pattern) beside them and, behind the All forms fold, their past, present, future and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 1479 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 1403 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms, pointing and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
